Learning to Trust

My husband got sober, but I was still angry and afraid. In Al-Anon, I began learning to trust my sponsor, my Higher Power, and eventually my husband.

By Celina R

Loving My Dad

Growing up in an alcoholic home was very interesting at times. It was fun and exciting, but it could also be very scary.

When my dad came home drunk, my mom would wake me up because sometimes he got violent and fought with her. She would say, “Can you help me put your dad to sleep?”

My job was to make sure I didn’t say anything to upset him. I would try to make him happy and convince him, “Let’s just get in bed. Let’s just go take a nap.” Once he was asleep, I would get his wallet out and take enough money for groceries, making sure some money was left.

Thinking about those nights, I still miss the smell of cigarettes because he always smelled like cigarettes.

My childhood was hard, but it was happy too. When he started drinking, my dad was fun. He loved music and dancing. We would dance and have fun, but by the end, he would be so drunk that he would get upset about little things. That would put me on alert mode, making sure I didn’t do anything that could upset him.

Growing up, I learned that you don’t tell anybody what happens at home. You never ask for help because people don’t really want to help you, or if they do, it comes with judgment.

My mom would say, “If you’re going to do something, you better do it right.” That’s part of the perfectionist in me, which I’m really working on. I would always try to be prepared. I knew that you always had to have money hidden somewhere, and you made sure no one in your family knew about it.

When I was eleven, before my parents separated, my dad got sober. He started going to AA. I remember going with him, and my mom would cook food for the meeting.

During his drinking years, he got himself a second family, and after he got sober, he left us to be with that family. So I knew people could be sober, but I still felt like I couldn’t trust them. I felt like they were still capable of abandoning you.

“So I knew people could be sober, but I still felt like I couldn’t trust them.”

After high school, I got a full-time job and started college. Every weekend I went out dancing. I never drank. I was so paranoid at the clubs that if I got thirsty, I would go to my car, get a drink of water, and come back.

When I started dating, I looked for men who did not do drugs. If they drank, it had to be minimal.

I would ask what they did for work, and I loved it if they had jobs that required random drug tests. I felt like it gave me security knowing that their employers had to test them.

I feel like those relationships took me nowhere, so when I met my sweet, really white, non-dancing husband who didn’t drink any alcohol—or so I thought—I was looking for something different. I feel like he was a bit of a risk because he was studying finance, and that job didn’t require any drug tests.

Keeping Up Appearances

Our first two years of marriage were really good. We were getting to know each other. He worked mornings, and I worked nights. We were busy trying to get through life. But our third year got pretty interesting.

His family loved getting together for Sunday dinners. My sweetheart would start saying crazy things, and after a while, he would start drooling and falling asleep at the dinner table. His family would ask what was going on.

My response was always something like, “What are you talking about? My sweet husband worked all night. He had so much work, and he’s just so tired. We need to let him sleep.”

I always prided myself on honesty, but I became a pretty good liar, keeping up appearances.

My husband had an office that the kids and I weren’t allowed in. He had very important papers, and we might mess them up. One day he was out, and curiosity got the best of me. I was hoping there were just papers in that office.

But I found hidden alcohol bottles. I couldn’t believe my husband had these things hidden. I poured everything down the drain and displayed the bottles in the kitchen, waiting for him to come home. I was ready for a fight. He needed to explain what was going on.

He was really calm. He said he had a hard time sleeping, and sometimes alcohol helped. He promised he would stop drinking, and I believed him.

Things got worse, so I kept investigating. I went through his text messages and found out he was buying drugs. He had an explanation too: the alcohol helped him sleep, and the drugs helped him concentrate on his work. He would tell me that lots of successful people did this.

To be honest, I think deep down I knew he was lying, but I wanted to believe him. I wanted to believe he was trying his best to be a good person. When I asked whether we should get help, he said he could do it on his own.

Through all this, I acted like nothing was happening. My kids looked good. They were clean. My house was in order. If you came to my house, you would think: perfect family.

Finally, he got into a car accident, was arrested, and got a DUI. This was my wake-up call. I knew we couldn’t do it anymore. We came clean to his family, and he went to rehab.

Some people say they feel good leaving their alcoholic in rehab because at least they know they’re safe. I felt hopeless and defeated. He had made so many promises and never changed. I had set rules and given ultimatums, and I was angry. I felt ashamed that all the men in my life had been a mess. I wondered whether it was my fault. The common denominator was me.

He Was Sober. I Was Still Angry.

After rehab, my husband was sober and doing better. Someone in AA helped him get a job. Now I had to start trusting him, but I just couldn’t.

We got him a phone, and I downloaded a tracking app. I needed to know where he was all the time. When he came home from meetings, I would smell him. He didn’t drink coffee, so if he smelled like coffee, I knew he’d been at a meeting. One meeting was at an Italian restaurant, and he would smell like Italian food. I was like a dog sniffing him all the time.

He kept going to meetings. He looked healthier and gained weight. His family was so proud of him. They would ask, “Aren’t you so happy he’s doing so much better?”

“Yes, I am. I’m so happy.”

But inside, I was thinking, “I wish I were a widow right now and people would feel sorry for me.” What was so glamorous about being married to an alcoholic?

In his second year of sobriety, I still resented him. I hated his guts. We had lost our home and our car. I had sold most of our furniture online. Two years later, we still had nothing. Only my kids got new clothes because they kept growing no matter what.

I still wanted out of the relationship, and I didn’t know how. I had these four rules: If he relapses, I’m out. If he hits me, I’m out. If he mentally abuses me, I’m out. If he hurts my kids, even if it’s a paper cut, I’m out.

I was always on alert, watching how he treated the kids and how he behaved. When was he going to say something mean to me?

He would come home happy from meetings, telling me what he had learned, and I would play along. I would intentionally pick fights with him, hoping he would act up. It sounds sick to think I wanted him to fail, but at the time, I just didn’t see another way out. I was really, really miserable.

“I would intentionally pick fights with him, hoping he would act up.”

I complained that he went to so many meetings. He should have been spending time with the kids and me. What wisdom did those AA people have that I didn’t? I was his wife. I had all the wisdom in the world.

I Wasn’t the Problem

When he mentioned a program for families of alcoholics, I was offended. He had decided to drink and use drugs. He needed help. I didn’t. I was good.

In summer 2018, I went to two Al-Anon meetings. People were crying and putting their dirty laundry out there for everybody to hear. I thought, “You’re a mess. You all really need help. I’m not like any of you. I never cry in public.” I wasn’t going back.

But my husband kept encouraging me to try different meetings. I would go and show him I didn’t need them. I wasn’t the problem. He was.

I went to a Wednesday night meeting, and those people were saying everything I had been saying in my head that I had never been able to say out loud. I felt so at home.

Me, Myself, and I

I kept attending. I could share, and afterward nobody would judge me or tell me what I needed to do. I started hearing about the Twelve Steps, and someone showed me the workbooks. I thought, “I can do this by myself. I’m taking online classes.”

I would answer the questions after each Step. Me, myself, and I—we were an awesome team.

Then a woman shared how important it was to work the Steps with a sponsor. I was offended. It felt like a personal attack. I was getting better. Hello! I didn’t need a sponsor.

But I found someone who was so calm. I felt like she could see the world ending and just say, “I’m ready for my meeting. I’m ready to go.” I loved that about her, and I asked her to be my sponsor.

We met in a study room at the library. I was ranting about how my alcoholic husband had ruined my life and how horrible things were. At the end, she said, “Our time is up. Next week, I may not remember everything you said.”

What? Wasn’t she going to remember? That meant she wasn’t going to tell her family what I’d said and how crazy I was. Those words gave me so much freedom.

Well, she does remember things. I started to share with her my darkest thoughts. She was the first person I think I really learned to trust.

I hated Step One. Accepting that I was powerless? No. That’s why there are rules and regulations. You follow them. That’s a way of having control.

I had thought about God growing up, but I didn’t rely on Him. He worked really slowly, and I needed answers right away. I had to learn patience. My sponsor suggested listing qualities I wanted in a Higher Power. My first thought was blue eyes, early forties, blond, and no facial hair. I think I was looking for a new husband instead of a Higher Power.

We put those thoughts aside and started writing the real things. My Higher Power never abandons me. He’s patient, and He doesn’t control me. I’ve really learned to trust Him.

Step Four was brutal. It took months. I don’t think I had ever cried so much. It helped me realize my part in the dysfunction of my family. I didn’t like seeing that.

But I knew the program was working because I was getting lighter and lighter. I could be honest with others and myself. I didn’t have to act as if I had it together. I didn’t have to act happy anymore.

Before Al-Anon, I never asked for help. Now I was constantly asking for help. I also realized I didn’t need to know everything, and not knowing something didn’t mean I hadn’t worked hard enough. Instead, I had room to learn.

“Before Al-Anon, I never asked for help. Now I was constantly asking for help.”

The Steps opened a new way of life for me. They taught me how to navigate the ups and downs of life. They taught me to be kind to myself and others. I don’t necessarily like making amends, so I try to slow down my thoughts before I open my mouth. I still make mistakes, but in this program, it is progress, not perfection.

The Day I Had No Control

After a few years in Al-Anon, life was so much better. One day, I had a medical emergency.

On the way to the hospital, my thoughts were racing. I was thinking about my kids and who would stay with them. My husband suggested someone in AA.

A few years earlier, my first thought would have been, “What an awful idea. We can’t trust an alcoholic.” But that day, when he said who he was calling, I felt so much peace. I loved that alcoholic and his family. I knew my kids would be safe with him.

I had never thought I could really trust my alcoholic husband, and definitely not with my life. After everything we’d been through, I always thought that one day he would be in a hospital bed and I would be the one making the decisions.

That day, I was the one in the hospital bed. I had no control over what was happening to me. But I was at peace. I knew I could trust my husband with whatever decisions he needed to make. I knew my kids were safe, and I trusted my Higher Power.

I Still Have Crazy Moments

Nowhere in the program does it say that if I come to meetings and work the Steps, my life will be perfect and all my relationships will be good. I still have crazy moments.

One day, I was wrapping presents and couldn’t find the tape. My husband works from home now and has an office I’m allowed to enter whenever I want. The man doesn’t use paper. He does everything online. But I thought he might have tape.

I opened a few drawers. Then I started going through all his stuff, lifting things, checking under the seat, and looking behind the computer. By the time I’d ripped the room apart, I had forgotten I was looking for tape.

I talked to my sponsor about my little relapse. She said I should make amends. So I told him, “My sponsor says I need to make amends to you.”

He thought it was something serious, like I had blown a bunch of money. I told him what happened, and he started laughing. “I don’t care. You can go through my stuff.” We both laughed so hard.

Today, we both work our programs. We both have sponsors we can call, and we keep working the Steps.

I never thought I would be able to trust my husband again. Honestly, I didn’t think I could trust anyone. But Al-Anon taught me how to be honest with myself, how to ask for help, how to love, and most importantly, how to trust.

I learned that trust doesn’t mean everything will always be perfect. It means I don’t have to control everything or be afraid of what might happen.

The Al-Anon closing says:

“We aren't perfect. The welcome we give you may not show the warmth we have in our hearts for you. After a while, you'll discover that though you may not like all of us, you'll love us in a very special way, the same way we already love you.”

That is how I feel about my Al-Anon family. We are not perfect, but I have learned to love and trust people in a way I never thought was possible.

I love my Al-Anon family, and I will always be grateful for this program and for everything it has taught me.

The Line I Kept Moving

I thought boundaries meant cutting my mother out of my life. In Al-Anon, I began learning where she stopped and I began.

By Lance W

One of the first things I learned in Al-Anon was about boundaries. I had none.

I thought setting a boundary with the alcoholic meant cutting them out of your life completely. It seemed like a harsh form of amputation. In Al-Anon, I learned that a boundary is where they stop and I begin.

Living with my mother was easy at first. I thought that was how our relationship was supposed to be. I did everything possible to make her comfortable and safe, giving her what she needed when she asked. I thought I was demonstrating my love for her.

I didn’t realize she had a problem until years later. By then, I was exhausted and worn down to the point that it felt as though there was nothing left of me. Mentally, I was confused, always trying to figure out why things didn’t work. Physically, I felt worn out, too.

The line kept moving

I can’t count how many times I said to myself, “This is the last time I’m going to do this for her.” Or, “If she does that or says that one more time, I will leave. I’ve had enough.”

I told her I couldn’t go through another rejection or being shut out again. But I always went back because I loved her.

The boundaries I tried to set never lasted. Somehow, they got lost in my thinking: “Can’t she see everything I’m doing for her and just love me?”

“Can’t she see everything I’m doing for her and just love me?”

The red line in the sand I had drawn was always moved just a little further back. I was the one paying the price. She kept doing what she wanted, and I was disappearing more and more.

I mattered, too

Then I found Al-Anon and started going like my life depended on it. I didn’t understand at the time how much I needed some kind of intervention. Al-Anon did that for me.

After several months, I started to realize that I was just as important as she was, but I was acting and living my life like I didn’t matter.

Setting boundaries became a way to show myself that I cared about myself. I started learning how to tell her no and mean it.

One dinner was enough

If I fixed a meal and she didn’t want it, I wasn’t going to run out, get something else, and fix that instead. She could get her own dinner. This was what I had made; she could eat it or not.

I began learning that I didn’t have to feel hurt by her choice or think I was a bad person because I hadn’t made something else.

Probably most important for me was learning to set limits when she told me I was worthless or didn’t love her—that if I did love her, I would do this or that for her. Through boundaries, I began learning that I could protect myself from that kind of treatment.

A pattern I didn’t want to repeat

Boundaries are tools I use almost every day. It feels good to be able to say no and mean it. The more I practiced, the freer I started to feel inside.

Without Al-Anon, the steps, and the fellowship of the people I met, I would still be stuck. My life might look the same—not necessarily with my mom, but in another relationship. The cycle would continue.

Al-Anon helped me begin to break that cycle. Boundaries are a major part of that help.

Voices from the Grave

Old family rules can follow you into adult relationships. Explore how Al-Anon helps you release their authority, find your voice, and live in the present.

By Lance W

Have you ever been haunted? Have you had an experience that left a memory so clear you find yourself reliving it long after it is over? Perhaps a parent, another relative, or a former partner has taken up residence in your mind. Their voice whispers what to think, say, and do. You may not recognize how much you have been living by those messages until you begin to see the pain they have caused in your life and how your choices have affected people you love and are responsible for. Al-Anon gives you tools to recognize how your life has been haunted.

The voice you are still trying to please

These hauntings can take different forms. You may still relive painful experiences with an alcoholic parent. Or the voice may belong to someone who never drank but controlled your life so completely that you still struggle to make decisions of your own. That person may have died, may be out of your life, or may still be part of it. The old rules can keep their hold in any of those circumstances. It is those rules and their authority over your life that need to be laid to rest.

A belief can become ingrained in you without your realizing you have learned it. Years later, it can still control your choices, making it difficult to hear your own voice or the guidance of your Higher Power.

A voice from the grave may be one you are still trying to please.

The rules you grew up with can shape how you try to earn love and approval in adult relationships. You may find yourself trying to rescue or save someone, or falling into the habit of mothering, managing and manipulating them. So much of your attention goes toward pleasing the other person that you lose sight of your own wants and needs. Over time, you can lose your sense of who you are apart from that relationship.

Al-Anon can help you see the connection between those old voices and rules and the way you treat yourself and the people you love today. You begin to recognize when you are making choices to earn their approval and how much of your own life you have set aside in the process. Seeing that pattern is the beginning of developing a life of your own.

The Al-Anon program is gracefully simple and patient. It offers a way to live your life and learn to make choices of your own. As you work the Steps, changes can take place so gradually that you may not notice them until you awaken one day to find that a part of your past no longer haunts you. If you are willing to commit to practicing the Al-Anon program, change can happen.

Put them right back in the grave

When an old voice returns and begins to rule how you feel or act, recognize that familiar danger zone. A judgment learned years ago is reaching into the life you are living today. You may still fear the consequences you once faced for speaking up or making a choice of your own. That fear can keep you obeying an old rule long after the experience is over.

Putting those voices back in the grave means letting go of the authority that past experiences still have over your life. You can acknowledge the hurt and pain and ask God to help you speak with confidence about how you want to live today. As you develop that relationship, you can begin to trust your own voice. The Al-Anon program gives you tools to remind yourself:

“I have lived by your rules long enough. Through my relationship with God, I am learning to trust my own voice and make my own choices.”

Past experiences may take time to lose their hold. As you grow in the program, those voices can grow quieter. When an old thought or pattern returns during the day, you can recognize it and put it back in the past where it belongs. “One day at a time” is how you practice living in the present.

Let go and let God

In Al-Anon, the Twelve Steps are key to letting go of a past that keeps you from living a life of your own. They help you get to know yourself without depending on approval from the voices that haunt you. With the program’s tools and support, you develop a relationship with the God of your understanding.

The key to living a life of your own, free from the rule of old pain and anger, is in your relationship with your Higher Power and your willingness to maintain that relationship.

The voices from the past can make it difficult to hear your Higher Power’s voice in the present.

It is a matter of willingness and turning your problems over to God. It is also a willingness to listen to and talk with God, seeking the direction and serenity that come from that relationship. Why keep giving those old experiences the power to rule your life today? The goal is to “Let go and let God.”

A God squad

Let the God of your understanding lift you up and sustain you every day. Your communication and relationship with God become the center of your program. Meetings help you find support as you listen to other members’ experiences and recognize something of your own life in what they share.

Your communication and relationship with God become the center of your program.

You can ask someone with experience in the program to be your sponsor: someone you trust who can take you through the Twelve Steps and listen when you bring them a problem. A sponsor helps you learn the program’s tools and put them to use. The Steps give you a solid foundation for your life and your relationship with your Higher Power.

If your sponsor is unavailable, you can turn to other members you have come to know and trust in meetings. Their experience, guidance, and encouragement can help when the haunts return. They can become your “God squad.”

When the past starts to haunt you

  1. Recognize the voice.

    Whose approval am I still trying to earn?

  2. Put its authority back in the past.

    That person’s judgment does not have to rule your life today.

  3. Find your own voice.

    Learning to trust my own voice.

  4. Let go and let God.

    Ask the God of your understanding for direction, and take time to listen.

  5. Reach out.

    Let the encouragement of someone you trust help you find your way.

Practice this one day at a time. Each time you recognize an old haunting, you can turn back toward the life you are living today.

A loving map of daily living

The Al-Anon program is a loving map of daily living. Along with the Steps and the help of others, it offers a way toward peace and a clearer view of your own life. As From Survival to Recovery expresses it: “Our sight, once clouded and confused, will clear and we will be able to perceive reality and recognize truth.”

This is a path to peace.

Your First Al-Anon Meeting: What to Expect

A welcoming, practical introduction to attending a first meeting: whether you belong, what happens, whether you need to speak, and what you might take away.

By Daily Paths

You may have found a meeting and still be unsure about going. Which door do you use? Will someone ask you to explain why you are there? What if you start crying and cannot finish a sentence?

You do not need to turn your life into a clear story before you attend. You can spend your first meeting listening. The customs and language will become more familiar as you hear people use them.

Arriving or joining online

For an in-person meeting, check the listing for the room and entrance as well as the address. Arriving a few minutes early gives you time to find your way. If people are already talking, a simple “Is this the Al-Anon meeting? It's my first time” can help you start a conversation without having to explain anything more.

Al-Anon does not require a referral or appointment. You can use your first name; there is no need to give the room your full identity or family history. The official newcomer FAQ explains these basics.

If you are joining online, allow a few minutes to connect and check your sound. Read the group's instructions about joining, cameras, and participation. A private place to listen helps protect everyone's conversation. If you are unsure how to take part, you might ask the host, “I'm new—how do people let you know they want to speak?”

What happens during the meeting

A member generally leads the meeting. Many groups begin with a quiet moment and the Serenity Prayer, followed by a welcome and readings about Al-Anon. There may be introductions and a few announcements before the main discussion. Al-Anon's suggested meeting format offers a common outline, while leaving room for groups to do things differently.

A speaker may describe their experience, or members may discuss a reading, a Step, or a topic such as resentment or acceptance. “Sharing” means talking about their own experience and what they are learning.

Meetings generally give people room to speak without interruption or advice. If you describe something painful and the next person shares their own experience, that can feel strange. You may have expected questions, suggestions, or an answer to your problem.

The practice is to listen and share experience, leaving each person to decide what applies to their own life. Someone's account of a difficult conversation may give you an idea to consider without telling you what to do. Al-Anon's guidance for groups encourages careful listening and avoiding advice.

You do not need to turn your life into a clear story before you attend.

Listening—and speaking if you choose

Speaking is optional. If you are invited to share, “I'm here to listen today” is enough. You can hear how others participate before deciding what you want to say.

If you do speak, begin with what brought you there: “I've been spending so much time worrying about someone else's drinking that I don't know what I need anymore.” If the words are hard to find, “I'm nervous, and I'm not sure where to start” is a beginning too.

Talk about what is troubling you today rather than trying to cover the whole history. If you become tearful, take your time. Pause to breathe, or say you would rather stop and listen for now.

As you listen, you may hear circumstances very different from yours. Someone may be talking about a parent while you are worried about a partner or child. Notice whether you recognize a feeling or a habit: waiting for the phone to ring, making excuses, or being unable to concentrate on anything else. The details do not have to match for something to be useful.

At my first meeting

I was very emotional in my first meeting. I wanted so bad to hear how to fix the alcoholic in my life. What I heard were people who were talking about themselves and their own lives. I heard them talk about what they had done for themselves how they had made changes in their own life where they had detached themselves from the alcoholic in their lives. What I left the meeting that day was people who had been hurt people who were angry talk about their recovery from the disease of alcoholism that had controled their life. I realized that they were talking about me. It wasn’t what I expected but the most important thing that I took away from my first meeting was hope. I came away feeling a little bit better than when I walked in. It was the feeling of hope, that there was hope for me kept me going back. They said to me at the end of the meeting to “ keep coming back it gets better.”

I did and it does!

— Lance W.

Words and customs that may feel unfamiliar

Hearing “God” or “Higher Power” may raise questions, especially if religion has been difficult for you or has never been part of your life. Al-Anon describes itself as spiritual and welcomes people of any faith or none. Each member is free to understand a Higher Power in their own way. Listen to how members describe that help in their own lives.

The readings can also sound unfamiliar when others seem to know them by heart. Give yourself time to hear what they mean. You might come back to one sentence later, after something in the discussion helps it make sense.

A few words you may hear

The Steps: Twelve principles that members practice over time as they work on their own recovery.

A sponsor: Another Al-Anon member who shares their experience of the program with you personally.

Anonymity: Protecting members' identities. Confidentiality also means keeping other people's stories within the meeting.

“Keep coming back”: An invitation to give yourself more time with the program.

Al-Anon's welcome for newcomers explains more about its spiritual approach, sponsorship, and privacy.

When a basket is passed around, the contributions help pay group expenses. Giving is voluntary; there are no dues or fees to attend.

Privacy is a shared responsibility: do not repeat who attended or what someone shared. Online, check what name your account displays and who can hear the meeting around you. Platforms differ, so ask the group if you have a privacy question.

When the meeting ends

The group may finish with a closing reading, prayer, or shared statement. Listen as others take part.

Members may stay to talk afterward, and Al-Anon encourages newcomers to ask questions before or after meetings. If something someone said stayed with you, that can be an opening: “I recognized what you said about worrying all the time. Could I ask you about it?” Or you could ask about a reading or word you did not understand. Online, ask whether there is time for conversation after the formal meeting ends.

You might leave relieved, or go home unsure what to make of it. Hearing people talk openly about things you rarely discuss can be tiring. Give yourself some time before deciding whether the meeting was useful.

The details do not have to match for something to be useful.

Groups differ in their format and atmosphere. Al-Anon suggests trying at least six different meetings before deciding whether the program is for you. That gives you a chance to hear different people and become more familiar with the experience. You do not have to describe the first meeting as wonderful to consider going again.

For help finding another meeting or exploring other support, see Finding Help: Could Al-Anon Be for You?. A Daily Reflection can give you a question to bring to your next conversation.

Choose a meeting to try next, or ask someone you met whether you could talk again.

Guide

Detachment with Love

Caring about someone whose drinking affects you without making their life your responsibility.

In this guide

  • When their life takes over yours
  • What detachment means
  • Practicing detachment
  • Caring without taking over
  • When guilt, fear, or pressure returns
  • When they are sober
  • Detachment and safety

When their life takes over yours

You listen for a change in their voice, watch their face when they come through the door, or lie awake rehearsing the conversation that might finally get through to them. If they seem happy, you relax. If they are angry, you wonder what you did wrong.

After a while, you make decisions around problems that haven't happened yet. You turn down an invitation because they might need you. You keep good news to yourself because they are having a bad day. Even when nothing is happening, you are waiting.

Detachment begins with recognizing how much of your life this has taken over. It means giving up the job of managing another person's drinking, moods, and choices so you can attend to your own. That applies whether the person is your partner, parent, adult child, sibling, or friend. They don't have to live with you to occupy most of your thoughts.

I don’t have to live on the edge of every decision you make.

What detachment with love means

Al-Anon's Detachment leaflet describes separating ourselves from the harmful effects of another person's alcoholism. Stepping back helps us see what is happening more clearly and turn our attention to our own well-being. It does not necessarily mean physical separation.

Distance alone doesn't settle the problem. You can hang up the phone and spend the next three hours arguing with the person in your head. You can refuse to speak while waiting for an apology. Their reaction is still deciding how you spend your evening.

With detachment, you begin to give that attention back to your own life. You can care about someone without supervising them. You can understand that alcoholism is an illness and still refuse harmful behavior. You can keep your plans even when they are unhappy.

“With love” includes respect for another person's right to make choices you would not make for them. In Al-Anon, this also means learning to trust a Higher Power with what you cannot control and seeking guidance for what you can do. Their recovery cannot be your assignment.

Practicing detachment

Understanding the idea is easier than following through when the phone rings. Start with a situation that keeps repeating.

Pause before responding

Notice what is pushing you to act. Are you afraid of what might happen, guilty about saying no, or determined to make them understand? A feeling can be strong without telling you what to do. Unless the situation is urgent, put down the phone or say you need time to consider the request.

The pause gives you a chance to decide whether anything is yours to do before agreeing to do it.

Stop the circular argument

You have explained your point several times. Now you are correcting each accusation and waiting for them to admit you are right. Ask yourself what another round will accomplish.

“We are going in circles. I'm stopping this conversation for now.” End the call or step away when it is safe. An issue that needs resolving can be addressed later; you don't have to keep arguing until the other person agrees to stop.

You don’t have to convince someone you’re right before you walk away from an argument.

Leave consequences where they belong

An adult sibling who misses work can contact their own employer. If you supply an excuse, you take on the task and hide the connection between their drinking and its consequences.

Stepping back means allowing consequences you have repeatedly prevented. It does not mean arranging a crisis or waiting for suffering to force someone into recovery. You cannot know whether a particular consequence will lead them to seek help. Immediate danger requires action; see the separate safety section below.

Resume your own life

Keep the appointment you would usually cancel. Eat a meal without checking your phone throughout it. See the friend you have been putting off. Concern may come along with you, but it doesn't have to cancel everything else.

Pay attention to sleep, food, and company as well. These needs are easy to neglect when each new problem seems more pressing than your own day.

Use the help available

At an Al-Anon meeting, you can hear how others handle situations like yours. A sponsor, an experienced member who helps you work the program, can help you examine a decision without making it for you.

Use the Serenity Prayer to ask what you need to accept and what is yours to change. When you cannot tell, ask your Higher Power for guidance, talk with someone, attend a meeting, or read program literature. You do not have to settle every difficult decision alone.

Caring without taking over

You can refuse a request and still be kind. You don't have to produce a warm feeling first; a brief, respectful answer may be all you can manage that day.

The blanket

In a familiar Al-Anon story, a woman shared that her husband often fell out of bed after drinking. She felt responsible for getting him back into bed, straining her back as she lifted him night after night.

After hearing about detachment at meetings, she proudly reported that the next time it happened, she had simply stepped over him and climbed into bed.

The response from the group helped her see another possibility: that was detachment, but where was the love?

The next time, she still didn't lift him back into bed. But before getting into bed herself, she covered him with a blanket.

She had found a way to stop rescuing him while still showing care. The blanket asked her to give neither her back nor her night's rest—just a little kindness.

You might decline another loan and still invite your sibling to lunch. You might sit beside your adult child while they make a difficult call, leaving them to speak. Help becomes taking over when you arrange the appointment, make the call, and check afterward to see whether they followed through.

There is also room for companionship that has nothing to do with solving a problem. Where contact is safe and welcome, enjoy the meal or the game. Every conversation need not become a discussion about drinking.

When guilt, fear, or pressure returns

Saying no may leave you feeling worse at first. Before changing your answer, examine the guilt. Did you neglect a responsibility or speak cruelly? Or is someone simply unhappy with your decision? Those call for different responses. You can apologize for how you spoke without agreeing to do the task.

Take fear seriously enough to examine it, too. Is someone in immediate danger, or are you trying to prevent an outcome you cannot control? Get help assessing the situation when you are unsure.

Other family members may want you to keep doing what they have come to expect. Explain what you will do, but don't turn the explanation into a request for everyone's approval.

You will sometimes check again, resume the argument, or agree to another rescue. Look at what drew you back in and talk it through with someone who understands. Grief may be part of this work: grief for the relationship you wanted or the years spent trying to change it. Feeling relief doesn't rule out sadness.

When they are sober

Sobriety can give you a new set of things to monitor. Are they attending enough meetings? Why are they irritable? Should you avoid raising a problem in case it upsets them?

Supervising recovery can become as consuming as monitoring drinking. Their recovery is still theirs to pursue. Your concerns still deserve to be heard, and trust will take more than a change in drinking to rebuild.

In Learning to Trust, Celina R. describes facing her own anger and fear after her husband's sobriety, and how Al-Anon helped her begin to change.

Detachment and safety

Safety comes first

Immediate danger or suspected overdose: call 911 in the United States.

If someone cannot be awakened or has slow or irregular breathing, get emergency help. Do not assume they can sleep it off. Learn the warning signs of alcohol overdose from NIAAA.

If opioid overdose is possible, give Narcan (naloxone) if available and call 911 immediately. Follow the product instructions and the dispatcher’s guidance. Stay until help arrives, even if they wake up. Narcan reverses opioid overdose; it does not treat alcohol poisoning. Learn about naloxone from the CDC.

Detachment does not mean accepting threats, violence, or unsafe care of children. You do not have to remain in a relationship or living arrangement to demonstrate love. If you fear someone’s reaction, get help making a safety plan.

National Domestic Violence Hotline: Call 800-799-SAFE (7233) or visit thehotline.org.

Begin with the next decision

Choose one responsibility you have been taking over and decide how you will handle it next time. Ask for help following through. Over time, doing less managing can leave you less resentful and more able to enjoy the person you care about. You can begin before they change.

Guide

Finding Help: Could Al-Anon Be for You?

A guide to recognizing the effects of someone else’s drinking, finding an Al-Anon meeting, and using the Steps, sponsorship, fellowship, and daily practice.

Is someone else’s drinking affecting your life? You keep the day running while privately worrying about tonight. Or the drinking stopped years ago, but you still watch other people’s moods before deciding what you need. Start with what this has cost you.

Al-Anon offers help to families and friends affected by someone else’s drinking. The person who drinks doesn’t have to seek help first.

Is Al-Anon for me?

How is the drinking affecting my life?

You cancel dinner because you can’t count on someone arriving sober, then explain another missed commitment. By evening, you’re listening for the door instead of enjoying what you had planned. These moments add up, even when you keep up with work and family responsibilities.

Questions worth asking yourself

  • Do I check on someone’s drinking or mood before making my own plans?
  • Have I taken on bills, responsibilities, or explanations because of their drinking?
  • Am I rehearsing one more conversation, hoping the right words will change things?
  • What have I stopped doing because I’m worried about what might happen?
  • Who knows how much this affects me?

These are prompts for reflection, not a test or a diagnosis. Al-Anon has its own self-assessment for adults.

On a good day, it’s easy to dismiss your concern. The person may hold a job, care about you, and meet many responsibilities. You can recognize those qualities and still be honest about the effect of their drinking. You don’t have to settle an argument about whether they’re an alcoholic before seeking support.

Why would I need help when I’m not the one drinking?

Perhaps you’ve spent enormous effort trying to help the person you love. Asking for help yourself can feel beside the point. Surely everything would improve if they would just stop.

But you’re living with the worry, anger, and uncertainty now. You need somewhere to tell the truth about how you’re doing. Hearing how others have handled similar situations may help you stop taking responsibility for things you can’t manage and see a choice that is yours to make.

You don’t have to wait for someone else to change before you begin your own recovery.

Seeking help doesn’t mean you caused the drinking or failed the person. It doesn’t decide the future of your relationship for you.

What if the drinking stopped, or happened long ago?

Sobriety may bring relief without immediately rebuilding trust or changing old habits. You may still check, anticipate trouble, or wait for a relationship to feel different. Separation or loss can leave questions you haven’t had room to address. Support remains available when the person no longer drinks or is no longer in your life.

Celina R. describes that gap in Learning to Trust: her husband was sober, but she was still angry and watching for trouble.

If you grew up around drinking, you may know everyone else’s needs more readily than your own. Perhaps saying no still feels dangerous, or you find yourself waiting for trouble when the house is quiet. Al-Anon welcomes adults affected by a parent’s drinking. Its assessment for adults who grew up with a problem drinker offers more questions to consider.

Young people need support too. Alateen is part of Al-Anon for teenagers affected by another person’s drinking. A teen can start with its self-assessment or speak with a trusted adult, such as a school counselor. No young person is responsible for getting an adult sober or holding the family together.

What is Al-Anon?

Al-Anon is a fellowship of relatives and friends whose lives have been affected by someone else’s drinking. Members meet to share experience, strength, and hope and work a spiritual program of recovery. It is separate from Alcoholics Anonymous: AA serves people seeking recovery from their own drinking; Al-Anon serves the people affected by someone else’s. Al-Anon’s introduction explains the fellowship in its own words.

Many people arrive hoping to hear how to stop the drinking. At a meeting, they hear members talk about their own lives: what they’ve tried, what hasn’t worked, and what they’re doing differently. That shift can be surprising.

The program brings together meetings, the Twelve Steps, sponsorship, and the wisdom members pass to one another.

How do I begin?

Find a meeting you can attend

Start with a time and format that work for you. Going to a room with other people may matter most; for someone else, an online or telephone meeting is the workable first step. Hybrid groups offer both an in-person gathering and an electronic way to attend. Check a listing’s details before joining.

  • In person or hybrid: Search the official meeting finder.
  • Online or by telephone: Explore Al-Anon’s meeting options.
  • For local help: Use Worldwide Al-Anon Contacts to find an information service.
  • For a teenager: Start with Alateen’s meeting information and check the group’s access arrangements.

If a listing leaves you unsure, ask the group contact: “I’ve never attended before. What do I need to know about joining?”

Before your first meeting

In person: Check the address, room, entrance, and parking instructions. Allow a few minutes to find the group. You can say, “This is my first meeting. Am I in the right place?”

Online: Check the time zone, link, passcode, and whether you need an app. Find somewhere private to listen; headphones help protect other members’ privacy. Read the group’s instructions about cameras and speaking.

Either way: Listening is enough at first. There’s no speech to prepare and no need to explain your whole family. Ask a question before or after the meeting if something is unclear.

What will happen there?

Meeting formats vary. A group may have readings, a topic, or a member speaking about their experience, followed by time for others to share. There are no dues or fees, though a group may invite voluntary contributions to cover expenses. Members are asked to respect one another’s anonymity and what they hear in the meeting. Ask about a group’s online privacy practices if you’re unsure.

You will hear references to God or a Higher Power. You don’t have to believe anything before walking in. Al-Anon is a spiritual program rather than a religious one, and members have room to explore their own understanding. Al-Anon’s newcomer FAQ addresses these and other common questions.

The separate article Your First Al-Anon Meeting: What to Expect walks through the experience in more detail.

What if the first meeting doesn’t feel right?

A first meeting can feel unfamiliar. Worry may leave you comparing your story with everyone else’s or trying to understand the language. Al-Anon suggests trying at least six different meetings before deciding whether it is right for you. Groups differ in size, format, and tone. Try another if the first isn’t a good fit.

Listen for something you recognize: a feeling you hadn’t named, a choice someone made, or a person you would like to talk with afterward. That may be enough to bring you back.

How does the program work?

Meetings and the wisdom of the fellowship

Reading about a principle can help you understand it. At a meeting, you hear what happened when someone tried to live it. A parent worried about an adult child may recognize the same urge to check and intervene that a partner describes. A story about no longer making excuses for a relative’s absence brings another choice into view. Their circumstances don’t have to match yours for the experience to be useful.

Members share what they have learned, including the times an old habit returned. No single person has the answer to your life. Over time, familiar faces and honest conversations give you people to turn to when a difficult moment comes between meetings.

The fellowship passes along what its members have learned by living it.

The Twelve Steps: turning toward your own life

The Twelve Steps are Al-Anon’s program of recovery. Working them with a sponsor shifts your focus from the alcoholic to your own life. You begin to see choices you hadn’t noticed and find new ways to respond to people and situations.

The Steps begin with accepting that you can’t control another person’s drinking. They invite you to seek help from a Higher Power, take an honest look at your own behavior, become willing to change, and make amends where you have caused harm. Later Steps bring that honesty into ordinary days through continuing inventory, prayer and meditation, and sharing what you have learned.

This isn’t a course to finish before you qualify for help. Members return to the Steps as they grow. Read Al-Anon’s official wording of the Twelve Steps and explore them with a sponsor.

Sponsorship: a conversation between meetings

A sponsor is an Al-Anon member who shares their experience of working the program with another member. When you’re deciding whether to make another call, offer money, or have a hard conversation, a sponsor is someone to talk with. That conversation helps you notice the fear behind your first impulse and consider a different response.

A sponsor shares experience; you make your own decisions. Listen for someone whose way of practicing the program speaks to you. Then ask whether they’re available and what contact works for both of you. Al-Anon’s sponsorship information explains more.

A spiritual program you can explore

For some, talk of God or a Higher Power is familiar. For others, it is a reason to hesitate. Al-Anon makes room for different beliefs and for uncertainty. You don’t have to borrow another member’s understanding to begin.

Spiritual practice can start with admitting, “I don’t know what to do.” Before another urgent call, pause and ask for guidance. Speak with a sponsor or another member, then decide what to do. The situation may remain uncertain, but you’ve given yourself time to choose your response. Accepting what’s happening today doesn’t mean approving of harmful behavior.

Other members can tell you what prayer, meditation, and a Higher Power mean in their lives. You remain free to explore what they mean in yours.

Taking the program into an ordinary day

The work doesn’t end when a meeting closes. An idea you understood there is harder to remember during an argument the next afternoon. That moment is where practice begins.

In the morning: Read a Daily Reflection or a passage from Al-Anon literature. Choose one principle to carry into the day. A prayer for guidance or a short gratitude list can help you hold on to that principle.

When something happens: Pause and ask, “What am I feeling? What’s my part? What choice is mine?” Call a sponsor or another member before returning to a familiar argument. A short note about what happened may help you see the pattern later.

In the evening: Look back honestly. What disturbed your serenity? Do you owe anyone amends? What did you do well? What are you grateful for? The day held more than its hardest moment.

The Daily Paths app offers reflections, prayers, a gratitude list, a journal, and space for a fuller evening inventory. Al-Anon also offers reading samples and First Steps audio. These resources support what you learn through meetings and conversations with other members.

Understanding a principle today doesn’t mean you’ll remember it every time. Bring the difficult moments back to your sponsor or your next meeting. There’s something to learn and another chance to practice.

Other help belongs in the picture

Al-Anon offers shared experience and ongoing support. A counselor, healthcare professional, or qualified adviser may also help with a concern that needs individual, medical, financial, or legal attention. These forms of help can work alongside meetings.

Other fellowships address related experiences. Adult Children of Alcoholics and Dysfunctional Families focuses on the effects of growing up in an alcoholic or dysfunctional home. Co-Dependents Anonymous focuses on relationships. They are separate programs with their own meetings and newcomer information.

When safety is at risk

Threats, violence, coercion, or concern for a child’s safety call for direct help. You don’t have to wait for a meeting or for someone else’s recovery before seeking protection.

If you’re in immediate danger in the United States, call 911. For help with relationship abuse and safety planning, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline: 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788. If your device may be monitored, use a safer device if possible. Outside the U.S., contact your local emergency or domestic abuse service.

One step today

Read the assessment that fits your situation, save the details of a meeting, or contact a group. If you go, a simple introduction is enough: “I’m new. Someone’s drinking is affecting me, and I’d like to listen.”

Guide

Setting Boundaries

Decide what you’ll accept, explain your limit, and follow through.

By Daily Paths

In this guide

  • Understanding Boundaries
  • Everyday Examples
  • Setting a Boundary
  • Step 4: Follow Through with Action
  • Step 5: Practice Detachment with Love

Living Without Boundaries

When asked how you are doing, your mind may immediately jump to how they are doing. You have been watching their moods, monitoring their drinking, and trying to keep their day from going wrong. You may have to stop and think before you can answer the question about yourself.

You say yes when you mean no, cancel your plans whenever they call, or give up sleep to have the same argument again. Each time, something of your own gets put aside. These habits can persist even after someone stops drinking, and they can return after years of practicing recovery.

Boundaries help you recognize your limits and decide what you will do to protect them. Begin with one situation where you keep setting your own needs aside.

Understanding Boundaries

You are powerless over other people, but you have total authority over your own choices. Setting a boundary means deciding what you will participate in, what you will take responsibility for, and when you will stop.

Keep these distinctions clear:

  • Boundaries are NOT ultimatums, threats, or weapons: A boundary is never meant to punish, lecture, or manipulate another person into changing. If your goal is to force someone else to stop drinking or act differently, you are attempting to exercise control, not establishing a limit.

  • Boundaries are NOT walls: Setting a limit does not require you to shut someone out of your life. You can refuse a conversation while they are drinking and still be willing to talk when they are sober. You remain open to a relationship while being clear about the behavior you will not accept.

  • Boundaries focus on your behavior, not theirs: For example, saying “You are not allowed to drink at this party” is an attempt to control someone else. Saying “I will leave the party if I feel uncomfortable around heavy drinking” is a personal boundary.

“A boundary states what you will do or tolerate, rather than dictating what the other person must do.”

Everyday Examples

A boundary becomes useful when you know what it means in a situation you actually face.

Ending a Conversation

The call has become another argument about whether they have been drinking. You have asked the same question and heard the same answer several times. You can say, “I love you, but I will not continue this conversation while you are drinking,” and hang up. You do not have to stay on the phone for circular arguments, verbal attacks, or drunken provocations.

Refusing to Cover for Them

Stop covering up the natural consequences of another adult's choices. When a hungover spouse asks you to call their employer, leave that call to them. The same principle applies when you are asked to pay another debt or clean up a mess they made. Decide what help you are willing to give instead of treating each request as your responsibility.

Having a Way Home

Never get into a car driven by someone who has been drinking, or let your children ride with them. Before attending an event, arrange a way home that does not depend on that person. Keep your keys and enough money for transportation with you so you can leave when you decide to.

Keeping Time for Yourself

“I'm going to bed at ten. We can talk tomorrow.” A consistent bedtime is a limit you can act on each evening. So is keeping your doctor appointment or taking half an hour to yourself instead of canceling whenever someone wants your attention. Put that time in your day and protect it.

Setting a Boundary

If you have spent years putting someone else's needs first, deciding on a limit may be easier than keeping it. Work through these steps with one recurring situation in mind:

Step 1: Notice Your Warning Signs

Your emotions and body are your best alarm systems. Whenever you feel overwhelming resentment, exhaustion, or anxiety, pause and ask yourself if a personal limit has been breached. Use the self-care acronym HALT: Are you Hungry, Angry, Lonely, or Tired? Resentment almost always signals that you have said “yes” when you wanted to say “no,” or that you are doing too much for someone else.

Choose one recurring situation to work on. What keeps happening? What does it cost you? What are you agreeing to that you no longer want to do? Naming a specific problem gives you something you can act on.

Step 2: Separate Your Responsibilities

Before setting a limit, clarify your responsibilities. Remember the “Three Cs”: You didn't cause their drinking, you can't control it, and you can't cure it. You are responsible for your own safety, health, and choices; you are not responsible for the alcoholic's sobriety, mood, hygiene, or consequences.

Before announcing a boundary, work out what carrying it out will require. Ending a late-night phone call may mean hanging up; leaving a gathering requires a way home. Choose an action you can carry out even if the other person refuses to cooperate.

Before you state your boundary

  • What specific situation am I addressing?

  • What limit do I need to set?

  • What will I do if that limit is crossed?

  • Can I carry out that action with the resources I have?

  • Who can support me when following through gets difficult?

Step 3: State Your Limit

State what you will do in a concise, matter-of-fact “I” statement, without preaching, nagging, or apologizing. When the answer is no, say it politely and firmly. For instance: “If there is screaming in the house tonight, I am going to take the kids and stay at my sister's.”

When it is safe to have the conversation, choose a time when you can speak plainly rather than trying to explain yourself in the middle of an argument. You can give a brief explanation, but you do not need to build a case that answers every possible objection. The point is to make your decision clear.

When safety is at risk

If you fear threats, violence, or retaliation, prioritize safety over announcing or defending a boundary. Make a personal safety plan with qualified support; ordinary boundary-setting advice is not enough in an abusive situation.

In the United States, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-SAFE (7233) or text START to 88788.

Call 911 if you are in immediate danger.

Step 4: Follow Through with Action

A boundary without follow-through is just an empty threat, which damages your credibility and self-esteem. If the limit you set is tested, carry out your planned action calmly and without malice. Do not enter into an argument justifying your boundary—simply follow through.

When they object. They may call you selfish, say you are overreacting, or insist that this time is different. You can acknowledge what they said and repeat your decision once: “I understand that you want to keep talking. I'm going to bed now. We can talk tomorrow.” Then end the conversation. Repeating the explanation until they approve can pull you back into the argument you intended to leave.

“You do not need their agreement to carry out your boundary.”

When you give in. Look honestly at what happened. Did you become afraid of their reaction? Did you want to stop feeling guilty? Had you chosen an action you were not prepared to take? Identify what got in the way and make a plan for the next time. Talk it through with a sponsor or someone you trust. One difficult attempt does not prevent you from following through today.

When the plan is not workable. If the person you planned to stay with is unavailable, you need another arrangement. If you announced a consequence in anger that you do not intend to carry out, replace it with an action you mean. Be clear about the revised limit. Adjusting a plan thoughtfully is different from abandoning it because someone objects.

Step 5: Practice Detachment with Love

Expect pushback when you change your behavior. Someone accustomed to your caretaking may resist losing it. Practicing detachment with love means allowing them to have that reaction without making it your job to settle their feelings.

When you feel guilty. After setting a boundary, you may replay the conversation or feel an urge to call back and make everything comfortable again. Before reversing your decision, return to why you set the limit. Ask yourself: Did I act against my values, or am I uncomfortable because I allowed someone to be disappointed? If you spoke cruelly, apologize for the words. You can take responsibility for how you spoke and still keep the boundary.

“You can care about their disappointment without changing your decision.”

Give yourself time to experience the discomfort without immediately acting to remove it. Call your sponsor, attend a meeting, or return to an activity you had planned for yourself. You do not have to spend the rest of the day watching for their reaction.

Judge the boundary by your own actions. Did you protect your sleep, keep your plans, or stop participating in an argument? Their continued drinking or displeasure does not erase that progress.

Choose one limit to put into action today. Use a Daily Paths reflection to keep attention on your own recovery as you practice.

Gratitude & Hope

Moving from despair toward appreciation for progress, even when circumstances haven’t changed.

“Hope is what gets us to the first meeting. Gratitude is what keeps us coming back.”

In homes affected by alcoholism, “gratitude and hope” can sound almost offensive. Grateful for what? Hopeful about what? When every day feels like waiting for the next crisis, the idea of being thankful can feel fake, and hope can feel like a setup for disappointment. Many people arrive in Al‑Anon with a long list of things that have gone wrong and almost no practice noticing what, if anything, is still working. ​

In early recovery, a lot of us live in constant complaint without even realizing it. We retell the latest disaster to anyone who will listen, rehearse old hurts in our heads, and scan for what’s about to go wrong next. In meetings, we hear others do the same and feel understood. But we also notice something else: members who have lived through very hard things and somehow talk about their lives with a different tone. They still acknowledge pain and loss, but they also mention small good things—sleeping through the night, a kind nurse, a funny moment, a clear “no” they were able to say. That mix can feel strange at first: honest about the hurt, but not only the hurt. ​

Gratitude in Al‑Anon usually starts very small. A member might be in the middle of legal trouble, financial mess, or fresh betrayal and still write down three things: “I have a place to sleep. The meeting is here. I didn’t scream today.” None of that fixes the big problem. But it shifts the focus from “everything is awful, all the time” to “this is hard, and there are still a few things helping me get through it.” Over time, that practice can soften the edges of constant despair. It doesn’t erase grief. It just makes a little room for something else to exist alongside it. ​

Hope in Al‑Anon changes shape too. At first, hope usually means, “I hope they stop drinking.” When that hope gets smashed over and over, many of us swing to the other extreme: “Nothing will ever get better.” In the program, we start to hear a different kind of hope—hope based on what changes in us, not on what the alcoholic does. Someone shares about still living with active disease but being less reactive, more honest, more able to sleep and laugh sometimes. Another talks about walking through a relapse with more tools and support than they had the last time. Hope gradually moves from “They’ll change” to “I can change, even if they don’t.” ​

The literature and meetings give us language for this: we can be grateful for a clear boundary we were able to set, not just for “good days” when nobody drank. We can have hope because we see small shifts in ourselves—taking one day at a time, asking for help, pausing before we react—not because life suddenly looks like a commercial. Members learn they don’t have to use gratitude to deny real pain. They can say, “This hurts, and I’m grateful I’m not going through it alone.” Both can be true at once. ​

As people keep showing up, they often notice that gratitude and hope act like fuel. On days when it feels pointless to go to a meeting or keep a boundary, remembering even one moment of relief or one sign of growth can be enough to take the next step. Hope doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine. It means believing that change—especially inside us—is possible, and that today doesn’t have to be a repeat of our worst yesterday. ​

In the middle of this disease, what are some small things you’ve learned to be genuinely grateful for—and how has that shaped the kind of hope you carry today?

The Stories We Tell Ourselves

Fear of rejection, uncertainty, and not being enough can shape the stories we tell ourselves. An exploration of seeing the facts and letting others help us face them.

By Neal W.

Someone cancels at the last minute, and we tell ourselves we didn’t want to go anyway. We cook a special dinner, and when they don’t show up, we excuse it by saying they’re busy at work. Someone’s drinking spoils another family gathering, and by morning we have an explanation for why this time was unusual.

We can be remarkably generous with explanations and excuses when we’re afraid of what people might think. Or what we might have to admit to ourselves.

Perhaps we’d have to admit how lonely we are, how hurt we felt, or how embarrassed we feel about what happened. Perhaps we’d have to face a disagreement we’ve been avoiding. Underneath it all may be a fear that is harder to say aloud: if we stop making allowances, ask for more, or let someone see how much we need them, they’ll reject us.

“It can feel normal not to know our own temperature, only theirs.”

That fear reaches well beyond anyone’s drinking. It can follow us into a friendship, a marriage, a meeting, or a room full of people we want to like us. The stories we tell often begin as a way to hide the truth from others. We want to look like we’ve got it together because we’re afraid to admit we’re struggling on the inside.

The explanations we need to believe

“They’ve been under a lot of pressure” may be true. But that pressure might be the consequences of their drinking. We say it to hide our disappointment. We dismiss the situation with a simple phrase that means we don’t have to explain our own experience.

Seeing things as they really are can be painful. We may have spent years believing things would settle down once work improved, the children were older, or the drinking stopped. There’s comfort in having a reason to wait. It postpones the question of what we would do if things stayed as they are.

“It lets us change without hating ourselves.”

Minimization, rationalization, and justification are the tools of denial. They help us avoid seeing the truth, telling the truth, or accepting the truth. Their language is familiar enough to pass unnoticed, especially when we’re the ones speaking.

How we explain it away

Minimization — making the impact seem smaller

“It was only one missed dinner.”

Rationalization — finding a reasonable-sounding explanation

“Work has been stressful. Things will settle down.”

Justification — defending a choice so we don’t have to examine it

“I had to cover for them. What else could I do?”

“I had no choice” can be particularly comforting. It spares us from making a choice we dislike: saying no, allowing someone to be disappointed, or admitting we couldn’t manage everything. We may have been afraid of their reaction. We may also have been afraid of who we would be if we were no longer the person who always understood, always helped, always made it work.

An explanation doesn’t erase the impact.

When fear fills in the blanks

The story doesn’t always comfort us. Sometimes fear supplies an explanation that hurts more than the uncertainty did.

A message gets a brief reply, and we read it several times, looking for what we did wrong. A friend spends time with someone else, and we wonder whether we’ve become a burden. Before anyone has rejected us, we’re already trying to make ourselves easier to keep around.

If we’re afraid we aren’t good enough, ordinary gaps in information can seem to confirm it. We apologize without knowing whether we’ve done anything wrong. We rehearse an argument about something the other person may never have thought. By the time we speak to them, we’ve been living inside that conversation for hours.

My first sponsor taught me to begin every difficult decision with a question: “What are the facts?” It’s a useful question when we’re certain we know what someone else is thinking, planning, or feeling.

A text goes unanswered. We feel hurt. But the fact is we don’t know why it hasn’t been answered. Keeping those things separate can be surprisingly difficult when the explanation feels so convincing. Our fear is real; the motive we’ve assigned to someone else is still a guess.

Sometimes we need more facts. There’s honesty in “I don’t know.” And one of the biggest things we don’t know is the future. We imagine that we understand all the possible outcomes of a decision. The truth, however, is that our Higher Power can create an outcome we couldn’t imagine.

Saying it where someone can hear

Something I heard in a meeting about thirty years ago has stayed with me:

“We tell others the truth because it makes it harder to lie to ourselves.”

There’s a difference between privately knowing we spent the weekend waiting and saying it to someone who cares about us. We hear ourselves describe the canceled plans, the checking, the excuses. We may start to add “but it wasn’t that bad” and realize how much work that little phrase is doing.

A sponsor remembers what we said last week, before we found a more comfortable way to explain it. Someone in a meeting describes making the same excuses, and we recognize our own reasoning before we have time to defend it. The recognition can be embarrassing. It can also be a relief to hear from someone who has thought the same thing or done the same thing.

We often find help in that shared experience. The person who has been through something similar may see a pattern more clearly because they’re no longer in the middle of it. They help us see through our story, just as they had to see through theirs.

What we already know

More information won’t always resolve the part that hurts. We may never know exactly why someone keeps breaking a promise. We may know quite clearly that we no longer trust it.

You don’t have to know what someone is thinking to acknowledge how their behavior affects you.

That acknowledgment can expose another story: if we understand them well enough, choose the right words, or become patient enough, we can make the relationship turn out the way we need it to. As long as the answer lies in something we haven’t tried yet, we can keep believing we control the outcome.

Accepting our powerlessness means facing the possibility that our best effort won’t change another person. There can be grief in that. We may have loved them, helped them, and done everything we knew how to do. We may still need boundaries we hoped would never be necessary.

When you catch yourself telling a story

  • Stop mind-reading. We can see what someone does and hear what they say. We can’t know what they’re thinking or feeling without asking—and sometimes we still won’t know.
  • Don’t argue with someone who isn’t there. An imagined conversation lets us supply both sides. We can work ourselves into anger or hurt over words the other person hasn’t said.
  • Put away the crystal ball. We tell stories about the future to explain or justify what we’re doing now. We can prepare for what might happen without telling ourselves we know what will.
  • Look at the facts. What do we know is true, and what do we only think is true? If we need more information, we can ask instead of filling in the blanks.
  • Say the story out loud. Tell a sponsor or someone we trust what happened and what we’ve made it mean. Someone who’s been there may recognize the fear or excuse we can’t yet see.
  • Face the fear and tell the truth. “I felt hurt.” “I’m afraid you’ll reject me.” “I’ve been pretending this doesn’t bother me.” With someone we trust, that honesty may bring the love and understanding we were afraid to ask for.
  • Let the truth change what we do. Once we recognize what’s happening, we can stop making the excuse, have the real conversation, or follow through on a boundary. We don’t have to control the other person’s response to be honest about our own lives.

    • We’ll never be perfect. We’ll still make assumptions and find excuses. We can admit we’ve been wrong without making it proof that we’re not enough. Learning to recognize the stories we tell takes time, and we’ll sometimes need someone else to help us see them. Each time we become willing to look again and tell the truth, we’re practicing recovery.
